# Node 26.11.1 lands with V8 15.5 and new stream draining

Big V8 upgrade, new stream dump APIs, and several crypto/sqlite fixes and refactors highlight the day.

### Node 26.11.1 release fixes docs (9899b39)

A small out-of-band release updated the changelog docs for 26.11.1.

### Major V8 15.5 upgrade and Node ABI bump (6b28cb0, 26cc118)

Node picked up V8 15.5.35.20, along with the matching `NODE_MODULE_VERSION` update to 152. This is the kind of runtime upgrade that can affect native addons and platform support, so it’s a meaningful compatibility boundary.

### `stream/iter` gets `dump()` / `dumpSync()` (9e6dd49)

A new pair of consumers drains iterable streams without retaining chunks in memory. That gives QUIC and other backpressure-sensitive code a purpose-built way to consume data to completion without paying the allocation cost of `bytes()`.

### Crypto key-sharing races were hardened (554dd55, d2a27ee, 3dbbdd0, 4775f2b, 71a657a, bacbcdc)

Several crypto paths removed mutexes or moved state to the right ownership boundary: EC PKCS8 encoding, verify setup, KEM, RSA-OAEP, secret-key initialization, and the root CA store. Together these changes reduce unnecessary locking and fix cross-Environment/thread-sharing bugs that could corrupt state or make concurrent operations flaky.

### SQLite now fails safely on oversized text (aa1bf2c, 4dfcf1d)

SQLite string conversion paths now reject inputs that would exceed V8’s string limits instead of aborting the process, and `enableDefensive()` now survives reopen cycles. These are practical reliability fixes for both error handling and connection lifecycle behavior.

### QUIC allocator state is no longer thread-local (0750039)

Each QUIC `BindingData` now owns its allocator state instead of sharing a per-thread singleton. This fixes mis-accounting and CHECK failures when multiple Environments share a thread.

### Native `ArrayBuffer` copy path switched to V8 fast-copy (a7e9f3b)

`copyArrayBuffer()` now uses V8’s native copy primitive and is exposed as a fast method. That should make buffer copying simpler and faster, especially on hot paths.

### Other misc changes

- Build fixes for V8 metadata, headers, flags, and illumos/Windows portability (10 commits)
- Benchmark CLI/runtime behavior updates (2 commits)
- Documentation and contributor-guide tweaks (4 commits)
- Test-only/supporting changes, lint rule updates, and dependency/vendor bumps (16 commits)

results.author: Philipp Esselbach
results.text:
Node.js 26.11.1 Released: A Three-Commit Patch That Is All Reverts

## Node.js 26.11.1 Released: A Three-Commit Patch That Is All Reverts

 Software 45028 Published 2026-10-08 08:31 by Philipp Esselbach

 Node.js 26.11.1 shipped with just three commits, and all three are reverts of documentation-tooling changes. The reverts undo a "move to redesign" of the build and doc pipeline, plus two dependent commits, and touch none of the runtime JavaScript APIs, networking code, or security paths. The real action happened earlier that same day with Node.js 26.11.0, a SEMVER-MINOR release that added Buffer helpers, stable process.ref()/unref(), HTTP header validators, HTTP/2's connectionWindowSize, perf_hooks histogram methods, and SQLite class renames. Meanwhile, the 26 line is still in its "Current" phase, with v24.21.0 listed as the Latest LTS, so teams should verify current status before upgrading. 

### Node.js 26.11.1 ships three commits. All three are reverts.

The newest Node.js patch undoes documentation-pipeline work from 26.11.0 and touches nothing in your runtime.

Node.js 26.11.1 landed on October 7, 2026 with three commits in its release notes, and every one of them is a revert. Release manager Antoine du Hamel pulled back documentation-tooling changes from the build pipeline. Not a single line of JavaScript went in. So if you were hoping for a feature, there isn't one. This is maintenance, plain and simple.

On paper, a patch release with three commits sounds about as thrilling as watching paint dry. That's kind of the point. Node.js runs on a strict semver model where the third number in a version signals a SEMVER-PATCH update: backward-compatible fixes only, no new features. Three reverts in one patch isn't a bug. It's the release manager doing exactly what a patch should do.

 

The three reverts are all about tooling, not code. du Hamel pulled back "build: toggle doc-kit verbosity based on V" (commit 2dc4638e85), "build, doc: move to redesign" (3febbc54ec), and "tools: bump the doc group in /tools/doc with 4 updates" (173250e2e7). That's the doc-kit verbosity toggle, the whole build/doc redesign migration, and a bump to several packages under /tools/doc.

None of them touch a runtime API, networking code, or anything security-sensitive. They're entirely about how the project builds and publishes its documentation website. And the pattern matters. When you revert a refactor, you usually have to unwind every change that leaned on it, which is why three related commits arrived bundled in one patch. Someone likely hit a snag and decided to step the line back to a known-good state before shipping. For what it's worth, this revert-in-a-patch pattern isn't unique to Node; the project rolls back problematic merges regularly, though three in one patch is on the quieter side.

#### The 26.11.0 release did the actual work

Hours before the patch, du Hamel also shipped Node.js 26.11.0, a SEMVER-MINOR release loaded with new features. If 26.11.1 was a quiet rollback, 26.11.0 was the noisy half. The "move to redesign" commit that 26.11.1 later reverted was itself one of 26.11.0's changes, a detail worth chewing on: the patch's entire job was to unwind a single documentation-pipeline migration from the day before.

The 26.11.0 notable changes, for those who want them:

Buffer. buffer.isLatin1() (#66298) detects whether a string uses Latin-1 encoding, and Buffer.stringLength() (#66064) computes byte length within a Buffer.

HTTP and HTTP/2. http.isValidHeaderName() and http.isValidHeaderValue() (#66334) are standalone header-token validators, while a new connectionWindowSize option (#65619) lets you tune HTTP/2 flow-control windows.

perf_hooks. monitorEventLoopDelay() got a resolution fix, RecordableHistogram can now record zero values, and two new methods arrive: histogram.diff() and histogram.snapshot() (#66098, #66099, #66114, #66115).

Process lifecycle. process.ref() and process.unref() graduated from experimental to stable (#6

# Node.js — Node.js 26.11.0 (Current)

Node.js 26.11.0 (Current) ships several SEMVER-MINOR additions: Buffer.isLatin1() and Buffer.stringLength(), new http.isValidHeaderName()/isValidHeaderValue() helpers, an http2 connectionWindowSize option, multiple perf_hooks histogram additions (diff(), snapshot(), hardened CBOR import validation, resolution truncation fix), graduation of process.ref/unref to stable, a new --process-timeout=N flag, renaming of sqlite's DatabaseSync and StatementSync, promotion of Alpine Linux to tier 2 support, and exposure of size/count in heap profile output for embedders exempting linked bindings from the addon permission. The release also bundles numerous bug fixes, performance improvements across buffer, http, stream, crypto, and ffi modules, and dependency updates including OpenSSL 3.5.9, npm 11.20.0, undici 8.11.2, and updated root certificates (NSS 3.129). Snapshot

Oct 07• 24m read time• From nodejs.org

Table of contents

Notable Changes Commits SHASUMS

Questions this post answers

What new methods did Node.js 26.11.0 add to the buffer module?

Node.js 26.11.0 adds Buffer.isLatin1() to check whether a buffer or string is valid Latin1, and Buffer.stringLength() to compute the byte length a string would occupy when encoded, without allocating the encoded buffer. Both are SEMVER-MINOR additions in this Current release. Developers tracking Node.js buffer API changes can follow release breakdowns like this on daily.dev.

Did sqlite's DatabaseSync and StatementSync classes get renamed in Node.js 26.11.0?

Yes, Node.js 26.11.0 renames DatabaseSync and StatementSync in the node:sqlite module as a SEMVER-MINOR change. The release also adds virtual table support via createModule(), rejects oversized string values, and restores connection state on reopen for the same module. Teams relying on node:sqlite can track API renames and breaking details via daily.dev before upgrading.

Is process.ref and process.unref stable in Node.js 26.11.0?

Yes, process.ref and process.unref graduate from experimental to stable status in Node.js 26.11.0. This SEMVER-MINOR change means developers can rely on these process control APIs without an experimental warning going forward. Keep up with Node.js API stability changes like this through daily.dev when planning upgrades.

# Node.js 26.11 Release: What Server Admins Should Check

Node.js 26.11 adds new APIs and changes SQLite, FFI and zlib behavior. Check these before you upgrade.

9 October 2026 · 4 min read · Kalesh Krishnan

Node.js 26.11.0 shipped on October 7, 2026 on the Current release line, and the 26.11.1 patch followed the same day. Current releases carry new APIs first, so production servers should stay on the LTS line for now. If you build tools, run CI pipelines, or maintain Node applications that will move forward later, several changes in this release can break existing code. This post covers what is new, which changes need attention, and how to test the upgrade safely.

## What Node.js 26.11 adds

The release adds a set of small APIs that are useful in server-side code:

- An `isLatin1` helper and `Buffer.stringLength()` in the buffer module.
- `http.isValidHeaderName()` and `http.isValidHeaderValue()` for validating header input.
- `histogram.diff()` and `histogram.snapshot()` in `perf_hooks` for working with timing data.
- `util.isPartialDeepStrictEqual()` for partial object comparison in tests.
- A `vfsArchive` option for single-executable applications, which serves bundled assets from a ZIP archive.
- Virtual table support in the SQLite module through `createModule()`.
- `process.ref` and `process.unref` have moved from experimental to stable.

## Changes that can break existing code

Most of the new features are additive. Three areas need a closer look before you upgrade.

### SQLite class rename

`DatabaseSync` and `StatementSync` have been renamed. The release notes do not give the new names, so read the 26.11.0 API documentation at nodejs.org/docs/v26.11.0/api before you change any imports. Any application that uses the SQLite module will need updating.

### Stricter FFI checks

The FFI module now rejects unsafe integers used as lengths or offsets, rejects non-boolean `copy` arguments, and throws type errors for invalid function signatures. Permission checks around `dlclose` and `dlsym` have also been removed. If your application calls native libraries through FFI, review each call site.

### zlib reset behavior

Calling `reset()` is now rejected after a gzip or deflate stream has emitted incomplete output, and while a zstd frame is still incomplete. Code that reuses zlib streams in a loop should be tested with truncated input.

## Security and dependency updates

Node.js 26.11.0 updates OpenSSL to 3.5.9, the bundled root certificates to NSS 3.129, undici to 8.11.2, and npm to 11.20.0. One permission fix matters for sandboxed code: a socket created from a file descriptor can no longer bypass the `allow-net` permission. CONNECT request paths are also normalized now.

The release page does not list CVE identifiers or describe an advisory, so treat this as routine hardening rather than an emergency patch. Rebuild any container images or binaries that bundle an older Node runtime so they pick up the new OpenSSL.

## Which release line should a server run

The Node.js site lists v24.21.0 as the latest LTS release, while v26.11.1 is the latest Current release. Current releases are for testing new features and catching breakage early. LTS releases receive long-term fixes and are the right choice for servers that must stay stable.

Use the Current line in a CI job or on a staging host so you find breaking changes before your production upgrade window.

## How TechProvidence can help

TechProvidence handles Node.js runtime upgrades on Linux servers, including staging tests, dependency audits, rollback plans, and moves between LTS lines. If you run several Node applications and want the upgrade done without downtime, contact us.

## Upgrade checklist

Work through these steps on a staging host before you touch production.

1. Check the versions you are running:

```
node --version
npm --version
```
2. Search your code for the renamed SQLite classes:

results.author: Philipp Esselbach
results.text:
Node.js 26.11.0 Ships With Native Process Timeout, Faster Text Tools, and SQLite Rename

## Node.js 26.11.0 Ships With Native Process Timeout, Faster Text Tools, and SQLite Rename

 Software 45028 Published 2026-10-07 18:21 by Philipp Esselbach

 Node.js 26.11.0 went live today with a native --process-timeout watchdog that automatically stops hung programs and reports where they broke, using the familiar Unix 124 exit code. It also adds faster text-handling helpers like Buffer.stringLength() and public header validators to speed up input validation and keep bad data from crashing apps. The long-requested SQLite class rename drops the Sync suffix, DatabaseSync becomes Database, without breaking existing code, since the old names stick around as silent aliases. As a normal feature-bearing update, it stays backward compatible with prior 26.x releases and quietly rolls in routine security upgrades to OpenSSL, npm, and V8. 

### Node.js 26.11.0 Lands With a Native Process Timeout, New Buffer Helpers, and a Cleaner SQLite API

Node.js 26.11.0 shipped today with a new way to automatically kill frozen programs, faster text-handling tools, and a long-requested rename of its database classes.

Node.js 26.11.0 went live today, and it's the kind of update that quietly improves what the runtime can do under the hood. Maintainer Antoine du Hamel shipped the release, and the changelog packs a native timeout feature, a couple of faster text-handling tools, and the long-delayed renaming of the database classes. Nothing here breaks. Most of it you'd only notice if you're actually looking.

 

Node 26, called Lithium, entered the "Current" line on May 5, 2026. This is a normal monthly feature update, so every change stays backward compatible and safe to use. Maintenance runs through 2029.

Here's the part that matters more than the version numbers: 26 is one of the last releases under the old yearly cadence. Starting with Node 27, the team moves to a single major release per year. It's a real shift, even if it doesn't feel like one yet. Funny aside: 26 is also the line that gave the project its "Rocket Turtle" mascot back in February 2024, though no one's quite sure how that connects to anything.

#### A timeout that sees what's going wrong

The biggest change is a built-in way to automatically stop a program that's hung. James M Snell added a --process-timeout flag that caps how long an entire Node process can run.

The motivation was simple. Existing timeouts were inconsistent across computers, and when they kicked in they didn't tell you why. You couldn't see the call stack, which is the part that actually helps you figure out what went wrong. Snell's answer is a background watchdog thread that interrupts the main program even mid-task, then prints the relevant details including where things got stuck, before exiting. It uses the same 124 exit code that Unix tools have used for decades, so it slots into existing workflows without a hitch.

There's a short grace period, and the flag has known quirks around the --watch and --inspect options. But for CI pipelines, containers, and quick scripts where a frozen process quietly burns CPU, this is the first timeout you can point straight at the runtime instead of bolting one on from outside.

The same idea of exposing internals shows up in the text handling. A new Buffer.stringLength() tells you how long a string would be before decoding it, which sounds minor until you're working with untrusted input you don't fully trust. You can size your memory budget first and skip the allocation if things look too big, which keeps a messy data feed from taking your app down. The benchmarks are strong: roughly 3.5 million checks a second for plain text.

Snell also added a fast way to check whether a string is a valid byte string. It runs roughly 221 million times a second on long strings, many times faster than a regular expression and thousands of times faster than a hand-written loop.

Node tightens builds and fixes tracing · Changelog

 nodejs/node · October 11th, 2026 · 10 commits 

# Node tightens builds and fixes tracing

Major simdjson integration, a diagnostics_channel context fix, and several build/runtime correctness updates landed.

### Update simdjson and stop dragging its headers through env.h (08a7e39, 2e9d43c)

Node upgrades simdjson to 5.0.3 and refactors inspector profiling to keep the large simdjson header out of broad transitive includes. That should cut parser overhead across many `src/` files and also changes how profile JSON is extracted and written.

### Fix diagnostics_channel callback context allocation (cbac135)

`traceCallback()` now creates a fresh context when none is provided, instead of reusing a frozen empty object. This avoids shared-state bugs when subscribers are present and aligns callback tracing behavior with the sync/promise tracing paths.

### Fix CJS package-map resolution for package imports (6b07f2f)

CommonJS resolution now skips package-map lookup for `#`-prefixed imports, letting `imports` entries resolve normally. This closes a bug where package imports could be incorrectly routed through the experimental package map instead of the package's own `imports` map.

### Keep gtest out of the node link line (3b639be)

The build now separates gtest's extra libraries from the main `node` binary link path, while still allowing cctest to use them. This reduces unnecessary link-time dependencies in the shipped binary.

### Support Python 3.15 in CI and configure scripts (85543c1)

Multiple workflows and configure entrypoints were updated to use Python 3.15. This is a build-environment compatibility update that keeps CI and tarball generation working as Python releases advance.

### Other misc changes

- Nixpkgs updates for tooling (2 commits)
- Doc tooling dependency bumps in `/tools/doc`
- Fix NAPI benchmark handling in GitHub Actions
- V8 cherry-pick to fix GCC 16 arm64 compilation

# Node.js 26.11.0 Released with New Buffer, HTTP, and Performance Hooks Features

🔄 Updated 6d ago

 Aggregated by BrevFeed releases · updated 6d ago 

#### Key points

- Added `isLatin1` and `stringLength()` to buffer module.
- Introduced `isValidHeaderName()` and `isValidHeaderValue()` for HTTP.
- Promoted Alpine Linux to Tier 2 support.
- Graduated `process.ref`/`unref` to stable.

## Core Module Enhancements

Node.js 26.11.0 brings several new features to core modules. The buffer module now includes `isLatin1` and `Buffer.stringLength()` for more precise string length calculations. The HTTP module gains `isValidHeaderName()` and `isValidHeaderValue()` functions, allowing for better validation of HTTP headers.

## Performance Monitoring Improvements

The `perf_hooks` module received multiple updates. These include fixing truncation for `monitorEventLoopDelay()` resolution, allowing `RecordableHistogram` to record zero values, and adding `histogram.diff()` and `histogram.snapshot()` methods.
